title: CRISPR/Cas9 gene therapy increases the risk of tumorigenesis in the mouse model of hereditary tyrosinemia type I

Background & Aims The therapeutic potential of CRISPR gene editing has been demonstrated in various animal models; however, little is known about its long-term consequences. This study seeks to bridge this gap by investigating the lasting consequences of CRISPR gene therapy in an animal model of hereditary tyrosinemia type I (HT-I). We compared the standard of care—nitisinone, a small molecule inhibitor of hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD)—with the deletion of the Hpd gene by CRISPR gene therapy. Both treatments block flux through tyrosine catabolism and thereby prevent the accumulation of toxic catabolites in HT-I. Methods We assessed the efficacy and safety of CRISPR gene editing in fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase-deficient ( Fah-/- ) mice, the mouse model of HT-I, 12 months post treatment with either nitisinone or CRISPR deletion of Hpd . We deleted the Hpd gene using an adenovirus containing Cas9 and an adeno-associated virus containing two sgRNA against the Hpd gene. Primary endpoints were survival, urine biochemistry, liver (immuno)histochemistry, and genetic analyses. Results CRISPR deletion and pharmacological inhibition of HPD both demonstrate efficient metabolic correction and rescue of lethality. Surprisingly, we detected a markedly increased incidence of hepatocellular cancer in the CRISPR gene therapy group (71%, 12/17 mice) compared with four control groups (nitisinone [19%, four of 21 mice], sgRNA only [6%, one of 16 mice], Cas9 only [11%, two of 19 mice], and hydrodynamic tail vein injection of both CRISPR constructs [24%, four of 17 mice]). All analyzed tumors in the CRISPR gene therapy group were deleted for Hpd but showed on-and-off target vector integrations. Conclusions CRISPR gene therapy increases the risk of hepatocellular cancer in the mouse model of HT-I. Because HT-I is characterized by inherent cancer susceptibility, this severe adverse event exposes the potential limitations of CRISPR gene therapy in cancer-prone disorders. Impact and implications Not much is known about the long-term consequences of somatic gene editing. Our study investigates CRISPR gene therapy in tyrosinemia type I using viral vectors. Although the CRISPR-based therapy effectively treated the metabolic condition, it was associated with a higher incidence of liver cancer than the current standard of care. These findings highlight the potential risks of using CRISPR gene therapy in conditions predisposed to cancer development. Graphical abstract Highlights • Hereditary tyrosinemia type I can be treated by deleting the hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase using CRISPR/Cas9 gene therapy. • CRISPR/Cas9 gene therapy cures metabolic conditions, but its use with viral vectors is linked to a higher incidence of liver cancer. • CRISPR/Cas9 gene therapy leads to integration of both adenoviral and adeno-associated viral vectors in liver cancer samples. Engineered CRISPR/Cas9 systems create double-stranded breaks in the DNA, which can be repaired by either homology-directed repair (HDR) or the error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) machinery. In the context of metabolic liver diseases, these CRISPR-mediated double-stranded breaks are mostly repaired by NHEJ owing to the quiescent nature of the liver, 3 which renders gene replacement or gene correction a challenging task. We therefore developed an alternative therapeutic approach known as metabolic pathway reprogramming, leveraging CRISPR/Cas9 to reroute an aberrant metabolic pathway. Rather than attempting to edit the disease-causing gene itself, this method introduces double-stranded breaks into a disease-associated gene, which will be deleted by NHEJ, thereby rendering the disease phenotype benign. 3 We and others demonstrated the efficacy of this therapeutic approach in a murine model of hereditary tyrosinemia type I (HT-I). 4 , 5 HT-I is a rare autosomal recessive disorder that leads to the accumulation of toxic metabolites resulting from the deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH), the enzyme that catalyzes the last step of tyrosine catabolism. If untreated, this condition can cause severe clinical consequences, such as liver and kidney failure resulting from metabolic decompensation, and the development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). The clinical standard of care is treatment with nitisinone, a small molecule drug inhibitor of hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase (HPD), the enzyme that catalyzes the second step of tyrosine catabolism. Nitisinone effectively reduces metabolic decompensation, but the pharmacological blockade is incomplete and dependent on patient compliance. It is therefore not surprising that nitisinone therapy only reduces but does not completely prevent the development of HCC. 6 , 7 Although metabolic pathway reprogramming in HT-I was proven to be an effective therapeutic strategy, 4 , 5 very little is known about the long-term outcomes of CRISPR gene therapy. The current study addresses this gap and reveals an increased incidence of HCC when using CRISPR in combination with viral gene therapy vectors while resolving the metabolic decompensation. Materials and methods Construction of DNA vectors Single-guide RNA (sgRNA) targeting the Hpd gene was used in our previous work. 5 The selected sgRNA-targeting sequences are shown in Fig. S1 , and further validation and characterization can be found elsewhere. 5 Annealed oligonucleotides (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) of sgRNA-targeting sequence were ligated into the pAAV 1179_pAAV-U6-BbsI-gRNA-CB-EmGFP vector from the Lagor lab ( https://www.addgene.org/89060/ ) using standard molecular cloning techniques. The pAAV vector was packaged into the AAV8 serotype and produced as we previously described. 8 The adenovirus (serotype Ad5) with an expression cassette of spCas9 (Ad5-CMV-Cas9) was produced by the Vector Development Lab of Baylor College of Medicine (Houston, TX, USA), as described on their website ( https://www.bcm.edu/centers/cell-and-gene-therapy/research/vector-development/technical-information/standard-operating-procedures ). Animal experiments All animal experiments were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. The tyrosinemic ( Fah −/− ) strain was kept on 16 mg/L nitisinone in the drinking water before experiments. Subsequently, 2.5 × 10 10 GC/mouse of AAV8_Sp_Hpd_I1/I3_CB_EmGFP (AAV-sgRNA-GFP) was introduced into 6–8-week-old mice of both genders by tail vein injection. Eleven days after the AAV introduction, 1.15 × 10 10 pfu/mouse of Ad5-CMV-Cas9 (Ad-Cas9) was injected via the tail vein in the same cohort of mice. Following the adenoviral injection, mice were weaned off nitisinone over 7 days and left without nitisinone for 12 months. In the control groups, 2.5 × 10 10 GC/mouse of AAV8_Sp_Hpd_I1/I3_CB_EmGFP or 1.15 × 10 10 pfu/mouse of Ad5-CMV-Cas9 were introduced into 6–8-week-old mice of both genders by tail vein injection. Mice were kept on 28 mg/L nitisinone for 12 months. Metabolic analysis Urine was collected over 24 h using metabolic cages (Techniplast, West Chester, PA, Cat# 3700M022). Urine succinylacetone was analyzed using standard methodologies as described previously. 9 Briefly, urine was mixed with an internal standard (13C succinylacetone; Cambridge Isotope, Tewksbury, MA, USA), and oximation was performed with hydroxylamine hydrochloride at pH >12, before adjusting pH to 1. The mixture was loaded onto a Chem Elut cartridge (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA Cat# 12198006), eluted with ethylacetate and diethyl ether, dried under nitrogen, and derivatized with Regisil. Trimethylsilyl-derivatized compounds were separated on an Agilent 6890 Gas Chromatograph with a capillary GC column. Detection was performed using electron impact mass spectrometry (5973 MSD, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Urine amino acid analyses were performed on a Biochrom 30 HPLC amino acid analyzer per standard protocols (Biochrom Ltd., Cambridge, UK). 10 Physiological amino acid standards were used to determine analyte concentration and analyzed using the EZchrom Elite software. Liver histology and immunohistochemistry Mouse liver samples were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde overnight for paraffin blocks. Serial sections of the same tissue sample were used to stain for H&E, HPD, GFP, F4/80, and trichrome. For HPD staining, sections were treated with citrate antigen retrieval solution (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA; Cat# S236984-2), and an M.O.M. Vectastain kit was used to perform the immunohistochemistry (Vector Laboratories, Newark, CA, USA; Cat# BMK-2202). Endogenous peroxidase was blocked using 3% hydrogen peroxide for 5 min. After blocking, sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with a primary mouse anti-HPD antibody (Santa Cruz Biotechnology, Santa Cruz, CA, USA; Cat# sc-271672) diluted 1:100 in M.O.M buffer. A biotinylated secondary antibody was incubated for 30 min. Detection of HPD was performed using a DAB detection kit (Vector Laboratories, Newark, CA, USA; Cat# SK-4100), and hematoxylin was used for counterstaining. For GFP staining, sections were incubated overnight at 4 °C with a chicken anti-GFP primary antibody (Abcam, Cambridge, MA, USA; Cat# ab13970) diluted 1:250 in buffer (PBS1x/0.5% BSA/0.2% Triton TX) and developed with an anti-chicken secondary antibody (Jackson ImmunoResearch, West Grove, PA, USA; Cat# 703-545-155) diluted 1:1,000. For F4/80 staining, sections were treated with citrate antigen retrieval solution and blocked with 10% normal goat serum. A rat anti-F4/80 primary antibody (AbD Serotec, Raleigh, NC, USA; Cat# MCA497) was diluted 1:250 in 1% normal goat serum and incubated overnight at 4 °C. A secondary goat anti-rat IgG antibody (Vector Laboratories, Newark, MA, USA; Cat# BA-9400) was diluted 1:200 in 1% goat serum and incubated for 30 min. Vector ABC Elite (Vector Laboratories, Newark, MA, USA; Cat# PK-6100) was incubated for 45 min, and staining was developed in DAB under the microscope (Biocare Medical, Pacheco, CA, USA; Cat# DB801). Trichrome staining was performed using Thermo Scientific™ Richard-Allan Scientific™ Chromaview™–Advanced Testing Masson Trichrome Stain (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA; Cat# IS87019). PCR and qPCR Genomic DNA was extracted from 20-mg fresh frozen liver samples using the DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Cat# 69506). PCR amplification was performed using Platinum SuperFi (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA; Cat# 12351010) and Phusion (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA; Cat# F530L) high-fidelity DNA polymerases. For reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), total RNA of tumors was extracted following the manufacturer’s protocol (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA; Cat# 1881060). Subsequently, 1 μg RNA of each sample was treated with DNAse and reverse transcribed using the qScript cDNA SuperMix (Quantabio, Beverly, MA, USA; Cat# 95048-100). RT-qPCR was carried out using the Applied Biosystems 7500, the iTaq Universal SYBR Green Supermix (BIO-RAD, Hercules, CA, USA; Cat# 1725120), and 500 nmol primers. Data were normalized using Gapdh. The amplifications were performed in triplicates for each biological sample. The primers used were as follows: Dicer1_ F: TCCTCGAAGAGGTGAGTTAATCGG, Dicer1_ R: GAGGCTCGAAGAGGTGAGTTAATCGG, Gapdh_ F: AGAACATCATCCCTGCATCCA, and Gapdh_ R: CAGATCCACGACGGACACATT. Detection of AAV integrations in tumor genomes of CRISPR-treated mice We aligned paired-end reads from each sample to the mouse (mm10) reference genome using BWA. 11 The resulting alignment was used to partition reads into two groups: reads mapped to the mouse genome with high quality (at least 250 matched bases with up to two mismatches) and reads that failed to align at this quality cut-off. Reads that failed to align were either discordant—with only one mate aligned to mm10—or unmapped with neither mate mapping to mm10. We then aligned unaligned mates from discordant mate-pair reads as well as both mates from unmapped reads to the adeno-associated virus (AAV) and Adenovirus (ADV) reference genomes using BWA. This analysis produced the following read classifications: (a) discordant reads, where one mate aligned to mm10 and the other to a viral genome; (b) failed discordant read candidates, where one mate aligned to mm10 and the other did not align to any reference genome; (c) viral reads, where both mates aligned to viral genomes with high quality; (d) soft-clip candidates, where one read aligned to a viral genome and the other read did not align to any reference genome; and (e) unmapped reads, where neither mate aligned with high quality to either reference genomes. Failed discordant read candidates (b) and unmapped reads (e) were discarded. Soft-clip candidates (d) were further interrogated using BLAT 12 alignments to mm10. Potential soft-clip mate alignments from these reads were clustered based on their aligned regions in mm10, and evidence for viral integration from at least three reads was used to define and support potential integration sites. Finally, evidence for viral integration from soft-clip reads required an alignment of at least 50 and 30 bps fragments for mm10 and a viral reference genome, respectively, from at least three reads with no mismatches. Lastly, we verified that evidence for integration—sequenced regions that align to mm10 and a viral genome—cannot be sourced from the same organism by aligning predicted viral regions to mm10 and predicted mm10 regions to the viral genome with relaxed stringencies. This pipeline identified 10 candidate integration sites that passed all the above criteria with evidence from soft-clip and discordant reads, including a site for AAV integration in Hpd at our CRISPR target sites. We stress that we expect that our predictions err on the stringent side and that this pipeline excluded some true integration sites. Sequencing data were deposited in the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA), accession code (PRJEB82105). Detection of recurrent deletions in tumor genomes of CRISPR-treated mice We detected large deletions using Pindel 13 and Delly2, 14 requiring events and regions to be predicted by both methods. All predictions that overlapped potential deleted regions in the wild-type control were excluded to avoid germline variants. Predicted regions were overlapped, and nine deletions that were detected in all four tumors from CRISPR-treated mice and absent in the wild-type mice were identified. In silico CRISPR off-target analysis We used the Benchling software ( www.benchling.com ; San Francisco, CA, USA) to generate the 50 best-scoring off-targets for each sgRNA (total of 100 off-target sites). According to the manufacturer, algorithms are based on two previous publications. 15 , 16 Because the software uses the mouse reference genome, we excluded potential Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms (SNPs) with our “normal mouse“ sequence sample. All 100 off-target sites had good coverage (36–45×) in all analyzed tumors. Results Effective treatment and metabolic recovery in Fah -/- mice 1 year after CRISPR gene therapy To develop a clinically translatable approach for metabolic pathway reprogramming for HT-I, we designed a method for long-lasting gene therapy in Fah -deficient mice ( Fah -/- ), the murine model for HT-I. We deleted Hpd by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing ( Fig. 1 A). We targeted the introns flanking exons 3 and 4 of the Hpd gene with two sgRNAs to induce an excision of the two exons. Because adeno-associated virus (AAV) does not have the size capacity to support two sgRNA expression cassettes, as well as the lengthy Streptococcus pyogenes Cas9 cDNA (spCas9), we used an adenovirus for the spCas9 (Ad-Cas9) construct and an AAV for the two sgRNAs and GFP as a reporter (AAV-sgRNA-GFP) ( Fig. S1 ). Fah -/- mice were injected with AAV (2.5 × 10 10 GC/mouse) followed by adenovirus (1.15 × 10 10 pfu/mouse) 11 days later to prevent potential interactions of the two gene therapy vectors. Thereafter, nitisinone was withdrawn from the gene-edited group (n = 17), whereas the control groups (noninjected, injected with AAV-sgRNA-GFP, and injected with Ad-Cas9 only) were kept on the drug (n = 21, 16, and 19, respectively). We previously showed that Fah -/- mice without nitisinone therapy survive only if the Hpd gene is deleted and otherwise succumb within 4 weeks. 5 Hence, the absence of morbidity and mortality beyond the first month after nitisinone withdrawal indicated that the Hpd gene was successfully removed in the gene-edited group. To analyze the long-term effects of CRISPR gene therapy compared with the control groups 12 months post injection, tyrosine catabolites were measured in blood and urine, and organs were analyzed histologically. The levels of tyrosine and phenylalanine in the urine were comparable in both groups ( Fig. 1 B). Most importantly, succinylacetone, the primary disease marker for HT-I, was significantly decreased in genetically treated mice compared with mice receiving nitisinone. Thus, the biochemical analysis demonstrated a sustained conversion of the deleterious tyrosinemic metabolite profile even 1 year post CRISPR treatment. Neither CRISPR- nor nitisinone-treated mice showed clinical symptoms of tyrosinemia and were phenotypically indistinguishable from wild-type mice. We euthanized all mice from all groups after 12 months and harvested livers to validate the efficacy of the treatment. The liver and body weights, as well as liver-to-body ratios, were similar in both CRISPR- and nitisinone-treated control groups ( Fig. 1 C). Immunostaining for HPD protein in the liver also confirmed that the enzyme was efficiently eliminated in the gene-edited group ( Fig. 1 D). Elevated incidence of HCC in Fah -/- mice treated with CRISPR gene therapy compared with the control groups To our surprise, we detected a significantly increased tumor incidence in mice treated with CRISPR gene therapy: 71% (12/17 mice) harbored at least one tumor, compared with only 19% (four of 21 mice) in the nitisinone group ( Fig. 2 A and B). Tumor formation was also markedly lower in all three control groups ( Fig. S2 ) in mice treated with CRISPR gene therapy, for example, 6% (one of 16 mice) in the AAV-sgRNA-GFP group, 11% (two of 19 mice) in the Ad-Cas9 group, and 24% (four of 17) in the hydrodynamic tail vein injection (Hydro) group ( Fig. 2 A). Hydro is an in vivo transfection method of hepatocytes, which maximally transduces 20–40% of all murine hepatocytes. 17 , 18 In-depth tumor analysis revealed that mice treated with CRISPR gene therapy had significantly more tumors per mouse. These tumors were on average larger (4.3 ± 0.7 mm diameter) compared with those of the nitisinone (1.2 ± 0.1 mm diameter), sgRNA (4.3 ± 0.6 mm diameter), and Cas9 (1.0 ± 0.0 mm diameter) groups ( Fig. 2 C). Histological analysis of CRISPR gene therapy tumors revealed typical features of HCC: cells with a high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and nuclear irregularities, tumor necrosis, and a trabecular growth pattern ( Fig. 2 D). Hence, tumors were distinct from regenerative nodules observed in patients with HT-I upon clonal expansion of corrected hepatocytes. 19 To rule out the accumulation of tyrosine catabolites in tumor cells, which potentially escaped gene therapy, we first wanted to ensure that Hpd was deleted in the genome of liver tumors, in addition to normal liver tissue, from mice treated with CRISPR gene therapy. HPD immunostaining was only reactive in the nitisinone group, and no HPD staining was detected in the tumors of the gene-edited group ( Fig. 2 E). It has been demonstrated previously that systemic administration of adenoviral vectors could activate an innate and adaptive immune response. 20 To exclude active inflammation and infiltration, we analyzed macrophage infiltration by macrophage staining (F4/80), which did not show any significant inflammation in either the nitisinone or CRISPR group ( Fig. 2 F). Furthermore, connective tissue staining (trichrome), as evidence of earlier inflammation and scarring, did not indicate any significant increase in liver cancer-associated inflammation 21 in CRISPR-treated mice compared with the nitisinone group ( Fig. 2 G). In summary, our data do not support a tyrosinemic or inflammation-mediated origin as a primary driver of liver tumorigenesis in mice treated with CRISPR gene therapy. Viral vector integrations and genomic deletions observed in mice treated with CRISPR gene therapy To further elucidate the pathogenesis underlying the increased tumor incidence, we performed genomic analysis. Because HCC is clonal and should allow for sufficient coverage, we applied an unbiased whole genome sequencing (WGS) approach to analyze four tumor samples and a syngeneic mouse control sample. Analysis of the Hpd locus confirmed the results of HPD immunostaining, revealing the predicted excision of exons 3 and 4 in all CRISPR tumor samples ( Fig. 3 A). Further, we identified discordant read pairs in the tumor samples, in which one end of the sequence aligned to the Hpd gene and the other to the viral vector sequences ( Fig. 3 B). Increased integration frequencies of the AAV vector when using CRISPR gene therapy have been previously reported 8 , 22 and have also been used to determine off-target cutting events. 23 , 24 Contrary to these studies, here we report vector integration in HCC, a severe adverse event of the therapeutic gene editing approach. We applied a stringent algorithm (see Materials and methods) to predict exonic and intergenic integrations in the tumor samples from CRISPR-treated mice ( Table S1 ). All integrations were confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing of the obtained bands ( Fig. S3A ). All amplified AAV junctions found in the Hpd locus and off-target integration sites either included the viral inverted terminal repeat (ITR) sequences or were located within 32 bp away from the ITR elements ( Fig. S3B ). Because GFP was detected in WGS, and the gene therapy vector contained a GFP expression cassette ( Fig. S1 ), we stained tissue from CRSPR-treated mice for GFP and detected multiple GFP-positive cells in the tumors and normal tissue ( Fig. 3 C). In normal liver tissue, hepatocytes were arranged in small groups with uniform expression levels of GFP surrounded by GFP-negative hepatocytes ( Fig. 3 C). This expression pattern is suggestive of integration of the GFP expression cassette and clonal expansion rather than sustained episomal AAV-GFP expression. In addition to AAV integrations, we also detected adenoviral integrations in the genome of CRISPR-treated mice. Interestingly, four of five integrations included a 103-bp inverted repeat of the ∼35-kb adenoviral genome ( Fig. 3 D). Even though these adenoviral repeats were not homologous to the AAV ITR sequences or murine integration sites, our findings indicate that inverted repeats might be preferentially integrated. When confirming adenoviral integrations by PCR and Sanger sequencing, we observed an insertion of an intergenic region from murine chromosome 4 in the Itih3 gene on chromosome 14, which was predicted by WGS to be an independent adenoviral integration ( Fig. S3C ). In addition to viral vector integration, we also detected genomic deletions. We identified nine deletions common to all four tumors subjected to WGS ( Table S2 ). Noteworthy is the deletion of the first exon of Dicer-1 across all tumor samples ( Fig. 3 E). Dicer-1 is a known tumor suppressor and has been associated with human and murine hepatocellular cancer. 25 , 26 We also detected reduced Dicer1 mRNA levels in three of four tumor samples ( Fig. S4 ). Interestingly, none of the off-target sites predicted using in silico methods coincided with the genes associated with observed viral vector integrations, genomic deletions, or insertions. Hence, current software tools, which are based mainly on homology to target sites of the sgRNA, 15 , 16 were not able to predict the complex mutational alterations that actually occurred in vivo . We did not evaluate CRISPR cutting in hepatocytes ex vivo , but the distinct chromatin structure would not be expected to accurately predict off-targets in vivo . 27 Discussion We previously reported the successful treatment of HT-I mice when deleting the Hpd gene by hydrodynamic tail vein injection of CRISPR/Cas9 gene-editing plasmids and thereby prevent flux through the tyrosinemia pathway. 5 This approach, referred to as metabolic pathway reprogramming, 3 was confirmed to be successful also by another group, 4 and we used it to develop a targeted therapy for glutaric aciduria type I. 28 In the present study, we aimed to extend our initial work in HT-I with a more translational gene therapy approach and a longer observation period. Although we could rescue all tyrosinemic mice using CRISPR gene therapy, we observed a surprisingly high rate of HCC (71%) after 1 year of treatment. The highest HCC incidence in the four control groups was found in the Hydro group, which was still three times lower (24%) than in the CRISPR gene therapy-treated group. It is noteworthy that both the Hydro and gene therapy-treated mice were not on nitisinone for a whole year, and hence, in both groups, an inefficient therapy with accumulation of toxic catabolites could drive tumorigenesis. Indeed, we previously showed that hydrodynamic tail vein injection with the same sgRNA against Hpd used here only produces a deletion in 20% of hepatocytes. 5 The edited hepatocytes have a growth advantage and eventually replace the nonedited hepatocytes. 5 However, the nonedited hepatocytes produce toxic catabolites until replaced, as flux through the tyrosine catabolism is not inhibited. Delivery of CRISPR molecules by gene therapy is more efficient than Hydro; however, the tumor incidence was much higher in the CRISPR gene therapy group. Also, all tumors in the CRISPR gene therapy group were Hpd deleted, inhibiting the accumulation of toxic tyrosine catabolites. In summary, these observations do not imply that toxic catabolites or accumulation of such in nonedited hepatocytes are the main reason for tumorigenesis. In addition to not being on nitisinone, the Hydro and CRISPR therapy groups are the only two groups exposed to functional CRISPR/Cas9 endonuclease activity. In the Hydro group, the CRISPR molecules were expressed from plasmids, whereas in the gene therapy group, they were expressed from AAV (sgRNA) or adenovirus (Cas9). It is well known that AAV can integrate into the target site when introducing double-strand breaks by zinc fingers or CRISPR. 22 , 23 , [29] , [30] , [31] We here confirm these results and demonstrate AAV integration into the Hpd gene locus as well as off-target integrations of AAV and even adenovirus. However, in contrast to previous studies, we sequenced tumor tissue and not primary cells. As far as we know, the present study is the first report of vector integration after CRISPR gene therapy followed by tumorigenesis. Although never reported in humans, previous animal studies on AAV gene replacement therapy have identified an increased incidence of liver cancer. 32 , 33 We did not detect any AAV integrations into the Rian locus, which has been associated with the formation of HCC upon AAV gene therapy in a mouse model of mucopolysaccharidosis VII. 33 , 34 In addition, our AAV and adenoviral control groups revealed the lowest HCC incidence. Therefore, we consider it unlikely that the gene therapy vectors per se , without the combination of CRISPR gene editing, increased the tumor incidence observed in our present study. Although we identified genetic alterations associated with human and murine hepatocellular cancer, 25 , 26 the present study cannot definitively determine the molecular modifications that lead to malignant transformation. A detailed evaluation of multiple sgRNA pairs, along with a comparison between all tumors and normal tissues, would be necessary. Nevertheless, the multiple control groups and 90 mice included in present study allow the conclusion that in this setting, the tumors in the tyrosinemic mice are caused by the combination of gene therapy and CRISPR gene editing. We can only speculate if different sgRNA target sites, another delivery system, or another metabolic disease would have generated the same outcome. However, the present study is a note of caution for metabolic liver disorders with tumor predisposition. We believe that a metabolic pathway reprogramming approach, as applied here for HT-I, could be successful for other metabolic disorders that do not have a predisposition for cancer. As promising as CRISPR gene therapy is, it is equally important to report all potential adverse events to increase the body of knowledge for safe clinical translation.
